Plain-English Definition: Continuing a policy for another term, often with updated price or terms.
Example: Your auto policy renews every six months.

Plain-English Definition: Notice from the insurer of the price and terms for the next policy term.
Example: You receive a renewal offer 45 days before expiration.

Plain-English Definition: Coverage that pays for a rental car while yours is being repaired after a covered loss.
Example: $40 per day for up to 30 days for a rental car.

Plain-English Definition: A claim that was closed but opened again because of new information or damage.
Example: A closed injury claim is reopened after new surgery is needed.

Plain-English Definition: Buying a new life policy or annuity that ends or reduces an existing one, which triggers extra disclosure rules.
Example: A replacement form is signed when switching life policies.
US Notes: States follow the NAIC Life Insurance and Annuities Replacement Model Regulation.

Plain-English Definition: The cost to replace damaged property with new property of similar kind and quality, without subtracting depreciation.
Example: Your 5-year-old TV is replaced with a new comparable model costing $900.

Plain-English Definition: A statement made by the applicant that they believe to be true, used by the insurer to decide on the risk.
Example: You state your home has a smoke detector.

Plain-English Definition: The minimum amount you must withdraw each year from qualified retirement accounts, including qualified annuities, after a certain age.
Example: At 73 you must start RMDs.
US Notes: The starting age is set by federal law (currently 73, rising to 75 in 2033).

Plain-English Definition: Cancelling a policy as if it never existed, usually because of material misrepresentation, with premium refunded.
Example: An insurer rescinds a life policy after finding undisclosed cancer treatment.
US Notes: The ACA limits rescission of health coverage to fraud or intentional misrepresentation.

Plain-English Definition: A letter from the insurer saying it will handle a claim for now but may later deny coverage.
Example: The insurer defends a lawsuit but reserves its right to deny if the act was intentional.
US Notes: Some states let insureds choose independent counsel (e.g., California 'Cumis counsel') when there is an ROR.

Plain-English Definition: How estimates of past claims change over time; adverse development means they grew, favorable means they shrank.
Example: Adverse development of $50M on prior-year claims.

Plain-English Definition: Money an insurer sets aside on its balance sheet to pay future claims and obligations.
Example: Reserves for unpaid claims and unearned premium.

Plain-English Definition: Benefits paid when you can work but earn less due to disability.
Example: You return part-time and receive partial benefits.

Also Known As: Assigned Risk; Shared Market; Market of Last Resort
Plain-English Definition: State-run or state-mandated plans that provide insurance to people who can't get it in the normal market.
Example: A driver with many violations gets auto insurance through the state assigned risk plan.

Plain-English Definition: Latin for 'let the master answer'. An employer is legally responsible for acts of employees done within their job.
Example: A hospital is liable for a nurse's error during a shift.

Plain-English Definition: The agent who deals directly with the customer.
Example: A retail agent works with a wholesaler for an unusual risk.

Plain-English Definition: The amount of loss kept by the insured or by an insurer before insurance or reinsurance pays.
Example: A reinsurer pays losses above the insurer's $1M retention.

Plain-English Definition: The percentage of policies that renew.
Example: An 87% retention ratio means 13% of customers left.

Plain-English Definition: The date on a claims-made policy before which incidents are not covered, even if the claim is made during the policy.
Example: A retro date of 2018 means a mistake made in 2016 is not covered.

Plain-English Definition: Reinsurance bought by reinsurers to protect themselves.
Example: A reinsurer buys retrocession for peak hurricane risk.

Plain-English Definition: The company that provides retrocession to a reinsurer.
Example: A hedge-fund-backed retrocessionaire.

Plain-English Definition: A plan where the final premium is adjusted after the policy period based on actual losses during that period.
Example: A large employer pays a lower premium after a year with few claims.

Plain-English Definition: Term life that refunds premiums paid if you outlive the term, at a higher price.
Example: After 20 years you get back all your premiums.

Plain-English Definition: How often, on average, a loss of a certain size is expected, such as once in 100 years.
Example: A 1-in-100 return period equals 1% chance each year.

Plain-English Definition: Money returned to the policyholder because of a cancellation or a reduction in coverage.
Example: Removing a car mid-term produces a $120 return premium.

Plain-English Definition: A federal crop policy covering loss of revenue from low yields, price declines, or both.
Example: Prices fall and yields drop; RP pays the difference.

Plain-English Definition: An add-on to a life or health policy that changes or adds benefits, usually for extra premium.
Example: A waiver-of-premium rider on a life policy.

Plain-English Definition: Coverage for drivers using their car for services like Uber or Lyft, filling gaps in personal auto policies.
Example: Covers the period when the app is on but no ride is accepted.
US Notes: Most states have TNC insurance laws.

Plain-English Definition: The chance that something bad and costly will happen. Insurers also use 'risk' to mean the person or property being insured.
Example: A house near the coast has a higher risk of hurricane damage.

Plain-English Definition: A program that moves money from health plans with healthier members to plans with sicker members.
Example: A plan with many diabetic enrollees receives risk adjustment payments.
US Notes: Used in ACA markets and Medicare Advantage.

Plain-English Definition: The types and amount of risk an insurer is willing to accept.
Example: An insurer's appetite excludes restaurants with deep fryers.

Plain-English Definition: A group into which applicants with similar risk are placed, such as preferred plus, standard or substandard.
Example: A non-smoker in excellent health gets Preferred Plus.

Plain-English Definition: The process of identifying risks and deciding how to handle them, such as avoiding, reducing, retaining or transferring them.
Example: A factory installs sprinklers and buys property insurance as part of risk management.

Plain-English Definition: Combining many people's premiums so that the losses of a few are paid from the money of many.
Example: Thousands of homeowners pay premiums into a pool that pays for the few homes that burn.

Plain-English Definition: FEMA's pricing method for NFIP policies, introduced in 2021, that bases premiums on each property's individual flood risk.
Example: Two neighbors pay different NFIP premiums based on distance to water.

Plain-English Definition: Choosing to pay for certain losses yourself instead of insuring them.
Example: A company pays small property losses under $25,000 out of its own budget.

Plain-English Definition: A liability insurer owned by its members in the same industry, allowed by federal law to operate across states after licensing in one.
Example: Physicians form an RRG for malpractice coverage.
US Notes: Created under the federal Liability Risk Retention Act.

Plain-English Definition: Choosing which applicants to insure to keep the book of business profitable.
Example: An insurer selects drivers with clean records.

Plain-English Definition: Shifting the financial cost of a risk to someone else, usually an insurer or through a contract.
Example: A contractor makes subcontractors carry insurance and name it as additional insured.

Plain-English Definition: Accounting tests to confirm a reinsurance contract transfers enough risk to count as insurance.
Example: An auditor checks there's a 10% chance of a 10% loss.

Plain-English Definition: A regulatory formula that sets the minimum capital an insurer needs based on its risks.
Example: An insurer below 200% RBC triggers regulator action.

Plain-English Definition: The USDA agency that oversees the federal crop insurance program.
Example: RMA sets crop insurance prices and rules.

Plain-English Definition: Coverage for towing, jump starts, flat tires and lockouts.
Example: A tow when your car breaks down.

Plain-English Definition: An endorsement paying roof damage based on the roof's age using a depreciation schedule.
Example: A 15-year-old roof is paid at 40% of replacement cost.
US Notes: Common in hail-prone states like Texas and Colorado.

Plain-English Definition: A book of business that no longer writes new policies but still has claims to pay.
Example: A closed-down asbestos portfolio in run-off.

Plain-English Definition: Damaged property the insurer takes after paying a total loss, or money recovered by selling it.
Example: The insurer sells your wrecked car at auction for $1,500.

Plain-English Definition: A vehicle title marking a car as having been a total loss.
Example: A car rebuilt after a flood has a salvage title.
US Notes: Rules and branding vary by state.

Plain-English Definition: A clause saying the insurer will not provide coverage or pay claims if doing so would violate sanctions laws.
Example: Cargo headed to a sanctioned port is not covered.

Plain-English Definition: A list attached to a policy that details specific items, locations, vehicles or people covered.
Example: A schedule lists 12 insured buildings with values.

Applies To Lines: Property, Casualty/Liability, Motor, Commercial, Financial Lines
Plain-English Definition: The part of the P&C annual statement showing how loss reserves have developed over ten years.
Example: Analysts use Schedule P to check whether reserves were adequate.

Plain-English Definition: Adjusting a commercial premium up or down within limits based on the underwriter's judgment of specific characteristics.
Example: A 15% credit for excellent housekeeping and safety programs.
US Notes: Maximum schedule credits and debits are filed with each state.

Plain-English Definition: Specific valuable items listed individually with their own limits, often with broader coverage.
Example: A $10,000 engagement ring scheduled on your home policy.

Plain-English Definition: A claim alleging violation of securities laws, such as misleading investors.
Example: Shareholders sue after the stock drops on restated earnings.

Plain-English Definition: A health plan where the employer pays claims from its own funds, usually hiring an insurer or TPA to administer it.
Example: A large company pays employees' medical claims directly.
US Notes: Governed by ERISA and generally exempt from state insurance mandates.

Plain-English Definition: When an organization pays its own losses from its own funds rather than buying insurance.
Example: A large employer pays employee medical bills directly and hires a TPA to process claims.
US Notes: Self-insuring workers' comp requires state approval; self-funded health plans are governed by ERISA.

Plain-English Definition: An amount the insured must pay (including defense costs) before the insurer becomes involved; unlike a deductible, the insurer doesn't pay first.
Example: A company pays the first $250,000 of each liability claim itself.

Also Known As: System for Electronic Rates and Forms Filing
Plain-English Definition: The NAIC's online system insurers use to submit rate and form filings to states.
Example: Product filings for a new auto program go through SERFF.

Plain-English Definition: A clause that applies the policy separately to each insured, as if each had its own policy.
Example: An exclusion for one insured's intentional act doesn't remove coverage for an innocent co-insured.

Plain-English Definition: The average cost of each loss or claim.
Example: If 10 claims cost $50,000 total, severity is $5,000.

Plain-English Definition: A cancellation where the refund is less than the proportional amount to cover the insurer's costs.
Example: Cancelling halfway through a $1,000 policy returns only $450.
US Notes: Some states prohibit or limit short-rate penalties in personal lines.

Plain-English Definition: A line where claims are reported and settled quickly, like property and auto physical damage.
Example: Hail claims are usually closed within months.

Plain-English Definition: Disability insurance that pays for a short period, often up to 3–6 months.
Example: Paid for 12 weeks after surgery.
US Notes: California, Hawaii, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Puerto Rico have mandatory state disability programs.

Plain-English Definition: Temporary health coverage that doesn't have to follow ACA rules and may exclude pre-existing conditions.
Example: A 3-month plan between jobs.
US Notes: Federal rules (2024) cap initial terms at 3 months; many states restrict or ban these plans.

Plain-English Definition: An older 4-digit industry classification still used by some insurers.
Example: SIC 5812 means eating places.

Plain-English Definition: D&O coverage paying directors and officers directly when the company can't indemnify them, such as in bankruptcy.
Example: Side A pays a director's defense when the company is insolvent.

Plain-English Definition: D&O coverage reimbursing the company when it indemnifies its directors and officers.
Example: The company pays a CEO's legal fees and is reimbursed.

Plain-English Definition: D&O coverage protecting the company itself, often only for securities claims in public companies.
Example: A securities class action against the company.

Plain-English Definition: A policy issued based on a few health questions, with no medical exam.
Example: A $100,000 simplified issue term policy.

Plain-English Definition: A document summarizing the terms of a risk, which underwriters sign to accept a share.
Example: Lloyd's underwriters stamp the slip for their lines.

Plain-English Definition: Coverage for losses when an employee is tricked into sending money to a fraudster.
Example: An employee wires $80,000 after a fake CEO email.

Plain-English Definition: Rising claim costs driven by larger jury awards, litigation funding and changing attitudes toward corporations.
Example: Commercial auto claims grow faster than general inflation.

Plain-English Definition: Government insurance programs funded by payroll taxes or contributions, like Social Security, Medicare and unemployment insurance.
Example: Payroll taxes fund Social Security.

Plain-English Definition: A federal program paying monthly benefits to people who can't work due to a severe disability and have enough work credits.
Example: A worker with MS receives SSDI.

Plain-English Definition: Exaggerating a genuine claim or lying on an application to pay less.
Example: Adding a laptop that wasn't stolen to a real burglary claim.

Plain-English Definition: A period when insurance is easy to buy, prices fall and terms loosen due to competition.
Example: In a soft market, brokers can get more coverage for less premium.

Plain-English Definition: An insurer's ability to pay all its obligations, including future claims.
Example: Regulators monitor solvency through capital ratios.

Plain-English Definition: Covers satellites during launch and in orbit.
Example: A satellite fails after launch.

Plain-English Definition: Damages for losses with a specific dollar amount, such as medical bills and lost wages.
Example: Hospital bills of $12,000 are special damages.

Plain-English Definition: A time outside open enrollment when you can enroll because of a life event like losing coverage, marriage or having a baby.
Example: You have 60 days after losing job coverage to enroll.

Plain-English Definition: A property coverage form that covers all risks of direct physical loss except those excluded.
Example: Most commercial buildings are insured on special form.

Plain-English Definition: An insurer's team that investigates suspected fraud.
Example: A suspicious fire claim is referred to SIU.
US Notes: Most states require insurers to maintain an SIU or anti-fraud plan.

Plain-English Definition: Coverage for unusual, complex or niche risks not handled by standard policies.
Example: Insurance for a film production or a rare art collection.

Plain-English Definition: Stop-loss that pays when one person's claims exceed a set amount.
Example: Pays one employee's claims above $150,000.

Plain-English Definition: A risk that could lead to a gain or a loss, such as gambling or investing. It is generally not insurable.
Example: Buying stock is a speculative risk because it can go up or down.

Plain-English Definition: Auto liability limits shown as three numbers: per-person bodily injury, per-accident bodily injury and property damage (in thousands).
Example: 100/300/100 means $100k per person, $300k per accident, $100k property.
US Notes: State minimums range widely (e.g., 25/50/25 or 15/30/5).

Plain-English Definition: Covers perishable goods that spoil due to power failure or equipment breakdown.
Example: A grocery's frozen food spoils in a power outage.

Plain-English Definition: A form your insurer files with the state proving you carry required auto insurance, often after a DUI or serious violations.
Example: After a DUI, you need an SR-22 for three years.
US Notes: Florida and Virginia also use FR-44 for DUIs with higher limits.

Plain-English Definition: An adjuster employed directly by the insurer.
Example: The insurer's own adjuster handles your auto claim.

Plain-English Definition: The contract between the FCIC and private crop insurers setting how losses and gains are shared.
Example: The SRA governs a crop insurer's risk sharing with the government.

Plain-English Definition: The state agency that licenses insurers and agents, approves rates and forms, and handles consumer complaints.
Example: You file a complaint against your insurer with the Texas Department of Insurance.
US Notes: Each of the 50 states, D.C. and territories has its own regulator.

Plain-English Definition: A value listed on the policy, but the insurer pays the lesser of that value or actual cash value.
Example: A car with a $20,000 stated value may still be paid at $15,000 ACV.

Plain-English Definition: The coding rules and formats insurers must use for statistical reporting.
Example: The ISO personal auto statistical plan codes each coverage.

Plain-English Definition: Sending detailed premium and loss data to statistical agents like ISO or NCCI as required by states.
Example: Monthly data sent to ISO under its statistical plan.

Plain-English Definition: The conservative accounting rules insurers use for reports to state regulators, focused on ability to pay claims.
Example: SAP requires acquisition costs to be expensed immediately.

Plain-English Definition: An insurer owned by shareholders who expect profits.
Example: A publicly traded insurer like Allstate.

Plain-English Definition: A scheme where investors arrange for someone to buy life insurance on themselves, intending to sell it to the investors.
Example: A senior is paid to take out a policy that is transferred to an investor.
US Notes: Prohibited in most states.

Plain-English Definition: Insurance that protects self-funded employers against unexpectedly high claims.
Example: Stop-loss pays for any employee's claims above $100,000.

Plain-English Definition: Handling a quote, policy or claim fully automatically without human touch.
Example: 70% of renters policies are issued with STP.

Plain-English Definition: Being legally responsible for harm even if you were not careless.
Example: A manufacturer may be strictly liable for a defective product that injures someone.

Plain-English Definition: An investment option in a variable policy or annuity, similar to a mutual fund.
Example: You split money among five sub-accounts.

Plain-English Definition: A smaller limit within the main limit that applies to a particular type of loss or property.
Example: A home policy may cap jewelry theft at $1,500 even though personal property is covered up to $100,000.

Applies To Lines: Property, Casualty/Liability, Commercial, Specialty, Financial Lines
Plain-English Definition: The package of information a broker sends an insurer to request a commercial quote.
Example: A broker submits applications, loss runs and financials for a manufacturer.

Plain-English Definition: After paying your claim, the insurer takes over your right to recover the money from whoever caused the loss.
Example: Your insurer pays for your car after someone rear-ends you, then sues the other driver's insurer to get its money back.
US Notes: Some states have 'made-whole' rules that limit health insurer subrogation until you are fully compensated.

Plain-English Definition: A request sent to a responsible party or their insurer to repay the claim.
Example: Your insurer sends a subrogation demand to the at-fault driver's carrier.

Plain-English Definition: Wording meaning damage must happen quickly and unexpectedly, not over time, to be covered.
Example: A burst pipe is sudden; a slow leak over months isn't.

Plain-English Definition: A clause saying the policy won't pay the full death benefit if the insured dies by suicide within a set period, usually two years; premiums are refunded instead.
Example: A death by suicide in year one results in a refund of premiums.
US Notes: Usually 2 years; 1 year in a few states such as Colorado and North Dakota.

Plain-English Definition: A requirement that an agent recommend annuities or policies that fit the customer's needs and finances.
Example: An agent documents why a fixed annuity suits a 70-year-old's goals.
US Notes: Most states adopted the 2020 NAIC Best Interest annuity model.

Plain-English Definition: A standard, easy-to-read summary of a health plan's costs and coverage, required by the ACA.
Example: You compare two plans using their SBCs.

Plain-English Definition: A document required by ERISA explaining an employee benefit plan's benefits, rights and procedures.
Example: Your HR portal has the SPD for the company's health plan.

Plain-English Definition: An additional request for payment when hidden damage is found after the first estimate.
Example: The shop finds a broken frame part and files a $900 supplement.

Plain-English Definition: Optional policies paid by employees, such as accident, critical illness or hospital indemnity, to supplement core coverage.
Example: An employee adds cancer insurance through payroll deduction.

Plain-English Definition: Costs the insurer pays in addition to the limit, such as bail bonds, court costs and interest.
Example: The insurer pays court costs and post-judgment interest.

Plain-English Definition: The company that issues a bond and guarantees the principal's obligation.
Example: An insurance company acting as surety.

Plain-English Definition: A three-party guarantee that one party (the principal) will fulfill an obligation to another (the obligee); if not, the surety pays and seeks repayment from the principal.
Example: A contractor's performance bond guarantees completion of a school.
US Notes: Treasury Circular 570 lists sureties approved for federal bonds.

Plain-English Definition: Insurance for risks the standard admitted market won't cover, placed with non-admitted insurers.
Example: A fireworks manufacturer buys GL in the E&S market.
US Notes: The Nonadmitted and Reinsurance Reform Act (NRRA, 2010) gives the insured's home state sole authority to tax.

Plain-English Definition: A specially licensed broker who can place coverage with non-admitted insurers.
Example: A broker places a coastal condo with a surplus lines carrier.
US Notes: Must file and pay surplus lines taxes in the insured's home state.

Plain-English Definition: A proportional treaty where the reinsurer takes the part of each risk above the insurer's retention line, in proportion.
Example: The insurer keeps $1M per risk and cedes the surplus up to $9M.

Plain-English Definition: A fee charged if you cancel a life policy or annuity in its early years.
Example: A 7% surrender charge in year one, declining yearly.

Plain-English Definition: A policy on two people that pays only after both have died, often used for estate planning.
Example: A couple buys survivorship life to pay estate taxes.

Plain-English Definition: A group of members at Lloyd's that underwrites insurance together, managed by a managing agent.
Example: Syndicate 2623 writes marine risks.

Plain-English Definition: An extra premium charged for higher-risk life applicants, often in steps of 25% above standard.
Example: Table 4 adds 100% to the standard premium.

Plain-English Definition: Another name for an extended reporting period, bought when a claims-made policy ends.
Example: A physician leaving a practice buys tail coverage.

Plain-English Definition: Professional liability for technology companies whose products or services fail and cause client losses.
Example: A software bug causes a client's billing errors.

Plain-English Definition: Technology that collects driving data like speed, braking and mileage from devices or phones.
Example: A fleet uses telematics to monitor drivers.

Plain-English Definition: Life insurance that covers you for a set period, like 10, 20 or 30 years, and pays only if you die during that time.
Example: A 20-year $500,000 term policy for a young parent.

Plain-English Definition: A rider adding term coverage for the insured or family members to a base policy.
Example: A child term rider covers each child for $10,000.

Plain-English Definition: A geographic area used as a rating factor because losses differ by location.
Example: Urban ZIP codes are in a higher-rated auto territory.

Plain-English Definition: Excludes loss from terrorism when the insured rejects TRIA coverage or for acts outside TRIA.
Example: A policyholder rejected TRIA; terrorism losses excluded.

Plain-English Definition: A federal program where the government shares insured losses from certified terrorist attacks above set thresholds; insurers must offer terrorism coverage.
Example: A commercial policyholder accepts or rejects terrorism coverage at binding.
US Notes: Reauthorized through 2027.

Plain-English Definition: Someone other than you or your insurer who may make a claim against you.
Example: A pedestrian injured by your car is a third party.

Plain-English Definition: A company hired to handle claims or administration for an insurer or self-insured organization.
Example: A TPA processes workers' comp claims for a self-insured employer.
US Notes: Many states license TPAs.

Plain-English Definition: Insurance that pays others you are legally responsible for injuring or harming.
Example: Your auto liability pays for the other driver's hospital bills.

Plain-English Definition: Data from outside providers used to prefill applications or enrich underwriting, like property characteristics or driving records.
Example: Prefill fills in square footage and roof age.
US Notes: Use of consumer data is regulated by FCRA and state rules.

Plain-English Definition: EPLI coverage for discrimination or harassment claims by customers or vendors.
Example: A customer alleges harassment by a salesperson.

Plain-English Definition: Protects property buyers and lenders against losses from defects in the property's legal title, like undisclosed liens.
Example: A forged prior deed is discovered after you buy.
US Notes: Paid once at closing; rates are regulated or promulgated in some states like Texas.

Plain-English Definition: Higher premiums for people who use tobacco or nicotine.
Example: Smokers pay two to three times more for term life.
US Notes: ACA allows up to 1.5x tobacco surcharge for health plans.

Plain-English Definition: A wrongful act, other than a breach of contract, that harms someone and allows them to sue for damages.
Example: Negligent driving that injures a pedestrian is a tort.

Plain-English Definition: The level of injury or cost that must be reached before you can sue in a no-fault state.
Example: You can sue only for 'serious injury' in New York.

Plain-English Definition: Paid losses plus case reserves for a claim or group of claims.
Example: Paid $30,000 plus reserve $20,000 equals $50,000 incurred.

Plain-English Definition: When insured property is destroyed or repair costs exceed its value (or a set percentage of it).
Example: A car with $9,000 damage worth $10,000 is a total loss.

Plain-English Definition: The percentage of vehicle value at which a state requires or allows a car to be declared a total loss.
Example: In a 75% state, $7,500 damage to a $10,000 car is a total loss.
US Notes: Set by each state, often 60–100%; some states use a total loss formula.

Plain-English Definition: A stack of primary and excess policies providing large total limits.
Example: A company buys a $100M liability tower made of ten layers.

Plain-English Definition: Protects businesses against customers not paying invoices due to insolvency or default.
Example: A supplier is paid when a retailer goes bankrupt.

Plain-English Definition: The kind of policy change recorded in a system, like new business, endorsement, cancellation, reinstatement or renewal.
Example: A 'REI' transaction reinstates a cancelled policy.

Plain-English Definition: Covers trip cancellation, medical emergencies abroad, lost luggage and delays.
Example: Illness cancels your cruise and you're reimbursed.

Plain-English Definition: A reinsurance agreement covering a whole class or portfolio of policies automatically.
Example: All homeowners policies in Texas are ceded under one treaty.

Plain-English Definition: Common dates when reinsurance treaties renew, such as January 1 or June 1 (Florida).
Example: Florida insurers buy cat reinsurance at the 6/1 renewals.

Plain-English Definition: Reimburses prepaid, non-refundable trip costs if you must cancel for a covered reason.
Example: A family emergency cancels a $5,000 trip.

Plain-English Definition: Persuading someone to replace an existing policy through misleading comparisons, to the customer's detriment.
Example: An agent exaggerates a new policy's benefits to earn a commission.

Plain-English Definition: The standard claim form (and 837I electronic equivalent) used by hospitals and other institutions to bill health plans.
Example: A hospital bills a stay on a UB-04.

Plain-English Definition: Latin for 'of the utmost good faith'. It is the legal principle that parties to an insurance contract must disclose all important facts honestly.
Example: Marine insurance law applies uberrimae fidei strictly, so an undisclosed fact can void the cover.
US Notes: In the US it is applied strongly in marine insurance under federal maritime law; other lines follow state misrepresentation statutes.

Plain-English Definition: The final total cost of all claims for a period once every claim is closed.
Example: Estimated ultimate losses of $80M for accident year 2024.

Plain-English Definition: Extra liability coverage above your auto, home or business liability policies, which may also cover some gaps.
Example: A $1M personal umbrella pays after your auto limit is used up.

Plain-English Definition: A neutral person who decides amounts on which the two appraisers can't agree.
Example: The umpire sides with your appraiser's $18,000 estimate.

Plain-English Definition: General claim department costs that can't be tied to a specific claim, such as salaries and office rent.
Example: Claims staff salaries are ULAE.

Plain-English Definition: Having insurance limits lower than the true value of the property, which can reduce claim payments.
Example: A house worth $400,000 insured for $250,000 is underinsured.

Plain-English Definition: Pays when the at-fault driver's insurance isn't enough to cover your injuries.
Example: The other driver has $25,000 limits; your UIM covers the rest.

Plain-English Definition: The primary policies that must be in place beneath an umbrella or excess policy.
Example: An umbrella requires $250k/$500k auto liability underneath.

Plain-English Definition: The person who evaluates risks and decides whether and how to insure them.
Example: A commercial underwriter approves a warehouse policy with a sprinkler warranty.

Plain-English Definition: The process of evaluating a risk to decide whether to insure it and on what terms and price.
Example: An underwriter reviews a restaurant's fire safety and loss history.

Plain-English Definition: The limits within which an underwriter or agent can accept risks without approval from someone higher up.
Example: A junior underwriter can approve policies up to $1M limit.

Plain-English Definition: The repeating pattern of hard and soft markets in the insurance industry.
Example: Profits attract capital, prices fall, losses follow, then prices rise again.

Plain-English Definition: An insurer's rules for which risks it accepts, declines or refers, and on what terms.
Example: The guidelines decline homes with roofs older than 20 years.

Plain-English Definition: Earned premium minus losses and expenses, excluding investment income.
Example: $100M premium minus $95M losses and expenses is $5M profit.

Plain-English Definition: Software that automatically applies underwriting rules to accept, decline or refer risks.
Example: Rule: refer any home built before 1950.

Plain-English Definition: A tool bringing together submissions, data, rules and workflow for underwriters in one place.
Example: An underwriter reviews a submission and third-party data on one screen.

Plain-English Definition: The year a reinsurance or London-style contract incepts; all its results are grouped to that year.
Example: Lloyd's syndicates close years of account after three years.

Plain-English Definition: The part of the premium for the time remaining on the policy; it would be refunded if the policy were cancelled.
Example: After 3 months on a $1,200 annual policy, $900 is unearned.

Plain-English Definition: A liability on the insurer's balance sheet equal to all unearned premium.
Example: An insurer holds $400M in UPR.

Plain-English Definition: A joint federal-state program paying temporary income to workers who lose jobs through no fault of their own.
Example: A laid-off worker receives weekly benefits.
US Notes: Each state runs its own program funded by employer taxes.

Plain-English Definition: State laws listing prohibited claim behaviors by insurers, like misrepresenting coverage or delaying payment unreasonably.
Example: An insurer fined for not responding to claims within the required time.
US Notes: Based on an NAIC model act adopted in some form by nearly all states.

Plain-English Definition: Charging different rates or treating people differently without a sound actuarial basis, or based on protected traits like race.
Example: Pricing based on religion would be unfair discrimination.
US Notes: Some states regulate AI and big data use in insurance, e.g., Colorado SB21-169.

Plain-English Definition: Prohibited behaviors in selling insurance, such as misrepresentation, rebating and unfair discrimination.
Example: An agent promises a policy is 'guaranteed to double'.

Plain-English Definition: A contract where only one side (the insurer) makes enforceable promises; the policyholder need not keep paying.
Example: You can stop paying premiums, but the insurer can't stop paying valid claims while the policy is in force.

Plain-English Definition: Pays for your injuries (and in some states damage) when a driver without insurance or a hit-and-run driver is at fault.
Example: A hit-and-run driver injures you; UM pays your medical costs.
US Notes: Required in about 20 states; must be offered in most others.

Plain-English Definition: Permanent life insurance with flexible premiums and death benefit, where cash value earns interest set by the insurer.
Example: You pay less in a tight year as long as cash value covers costs.

Plain-English Definition: Auto insurance priced using data about how and how much you drive, from an app or device.
Example: Safe braking earns a 20% discount.

Plain-English Definition: Insurers can start using rates and then file them within a set time.
Example: Rates used immediately and filed within 30 days.

Also Known As: Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act
Plain-English Definition: Federal workers' compensation for maritime workers such as dockworkers and ship repairers.
Example: A shipyard worker's injury is covered under USL&H.

Plain-English Definition: The amount a plan considers normal for a service in an area, used to pay out-of-network claims.
Example: The plan pays out-of-network based on UCR of $150.

Plain-English Definition: The plan's review of whether care is medically necessary and appropriate.
Example: A nurse reviews whether a hospital stay should continue.

Plain-English Definition: Both you and the insurer must be completely honest with each other, especially about facts that affect the risk.
Example: Hiding that you smoke on a life application breaks this duty and may void the policy.

Plain-English Definition: Reduces or removes coverage if a building is vacant for longer than a set period, often 60 days.
Example: A house empty for 90 days loses coverage for vandalism.

Plain-English Definition: Payment models that reward providers for quality and outcomes rather than volume.
Example: A provider earns bonuses for reducing hospital readmissions.

Plain-English Definition: A policy that pays a fixed, pre-agreed amount for a total loss, regardless of actual value at the time.
Example: A life policy pays $500,000 at death; nobody measures the 'value' of the loss.
US Notes: Several states have 'valued policy laws' requiring full face payment for total fire losses on buildings.

Plain-English Definition: An annuity where money is invested in sub-accounts and value rises or falls with markets.
Example: A VA invested in bond and stock funds.
US Notes: Regulated as a security by the SEC/FINRA and by states.

Plain-English Definition: Permanent life insurance whose cash value and sometimes death benefit depend on investment sub-accounts.
Example: Your policy value falls when the market drops.
US Notes: Sellers need a securities license.

Plain-English Definition: Universal life where cash value is invested in sub-accounts like mutual funds, with investment risk on the policyowner.
Example: Cash value rises and falls with chosen stock funds.
US Notes: Regulated as a security by the SEC and FINRA as well as by states.

Plain-English Definition: A code assigned to each vehicle model reflecting its loss costs, used to price physical damage and liability.
Example: A sports car has a higher symbol than a minivan.
US Notes: ISO and insurer proprietary symbols are used.

Plain-English Definition: Selling the life policy of a terminally or chronically ill person to a third party.
Example: A terminally ill person sells their policy for 70% of face.

Plain-English Definition: Being held responsible for harm caused by someone else, such as an employee.
Example: An employer is liable when its delivery driver causes a crash on the job.

Plain-English Definition: A unique 17-character code identifying a vehicle, used for rating and claims.
Example: The VIN decoder fills in make, model and year.

Plain-English Definition: Coverage for eye exams, glasses and contact lenses.
Example: A $10 eye exam and $150 allowance for frames.

Plain-English Definition: A policy that has no legal effect at all, as if it never existed.
Example: A policy on property you have no insurable interest in is void.

Plain-English Definition: A valid policy that one party may choose to cancel because of a problem, like a misrepresentation.
Example: The insurer may void the policy after discovering the applicant lied.

Plain-English Definition: A time that must pass before benefits begin or before coverage takes effect.
Example: A disability policy with a 90-day elimination period pays starting on day 91.

Plain-English Definition: Voluntarily giving up a known right.
Example: An insurer that pays a late-reported claim without objection may have waived the notice requirement.

Plain-English Definition: A rider that stops premiums from being due if you become disabled.
Example: After a stroke, your premiums are waived.

Plain-English Definition: An agreement that the insurer will not seek recovery from a certain party after paying a claim.
Example: A lease requires both landlord and tenant insurers to waive subrogation.

Plain-English Definition: Excludes losses caused by war, invasion or military action.
Example: Damage from an act of war is not covered.

Plain-English Definition: Separate coverage for ships, cargo or aircraft against war and related perils excluded from standard policies.
Example: A tanker transiting a conflict zone buys war cover.

Plain-English Definition: Extends cargo coverage from the seller's warehouse to the buyer's final warehouse, including land transit.
Example: Goods covered from a factory in China to a store in Chicago.

Plain-English Definition: A promise by the insured that certain facts are true or that certain things will or won't be done. Breaking it can void coverage.
Example: A jewelry store warrants that its alarm will be on whenever it is closed.
US Notes: Many states soften strict warranty law so a breach only voids coverage if it increased the risk or contributed to the loss.

Plain-English Definition: Optional coverage for water that backs up through sewers or drains or overflows from a sump pump.
Example: Covers a flooded basement from a failed sump pump.

Plain-English Definition: Gradual damage from ordinary use and age. It is almost always excluded.
Example: A worn-out carpet is not covered because it is wear and tear.

Plain-English Definition: Covers cancellation costs and liability for weddings and private events.
Example: A venue closes unexpectedly.

Plain-English Definition: Permanent life insurance with fixed premiums, a guaranteed death benefit and guaranteed cash value growth.
Example: A $100,000 whole life policy with level premiums for life.

Plain-English Definition: A broker who helps retail agents access specialty or surplus lines insurers.
Example: A retail agent uses a wholesaler to place a hard-to-insure nightclub.

Plain-English Definition: A score estimating a property's exposure to wildfire, used in underwriting and pricing.
Example: A home near dense brush receives a high wildfire score.
US Notes: California requires insurers to consider mitigation (Safer from Wildfires).

Plain-English Definition: Features that reduce hurricane damage, like hurricane straps and impact windows, which can earn premium discounts.
Example: A wind mitigation report saves 20% on a Florida premium.
US Notes: Florida law requires insurers to offer wind mitigation discounts.

Plain-English Definition: State-created insurers that provide wind coverage in coastal areas where private insurers won't.
Example: The Texas Windstorm Insurance Association covers a Galveston home.

Plain-English Definition: Insurance that pays medical care and lost wages for employees injured on the job, regardless of fault, in exchange for limiting lawsuits.
Example: An employee injured lifting boxes gets medical care and wage replacement.
US Notes: Required by state law (Texas lets employers opt out); North Dakota, Ohio, Washington and Wyoming have monopolistic state funds.

Plain-English Definition: An NFIP arrangement where private insurers sell and service federal flood policies under their own name.
Example: Your auto insurer also issues your NFIP flood policy.

Plain-English Definition: The total premium on policies issued during a period, whether or not it has been earned yet.
Example: Policies sold in 2025 total $50M written premium.

Plain-English Definition: The trigger for management and professional liability: an actual or alleged error, omission, misstatement or breach of duty.
Example: A board allegedly misled investors.

Plain-English Definition: Covers personal boats for damage and liability.
Example: A sailboat damaged in a storm.

Plain-English Definition: A federal crop policy covering loss of production (yield) below a guaranteed level.
Example: Hail cuts wheat yield by 40%.

Plain-English Definition: International rules for calculating general average contributions.
Example: The adjuster applies the York-Antwerp Rules 2016.
